lead: A single equilibrium stage splits a solute between two liquid phases in a ratio fixed by the tie line. One contact leaves plenty of solute behind, so the raffinate is contacted again with fresh solvent, stage after stage. Each contact cuts the solute by the same factor, giving a geometric fall that one formula sums. Cross-current extraction is used for batch recovery of vegetable oil, antibiotics and metal salts, and it is the simplest cascade to design and run.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for tie lines, the plait point and the distribution coefficient K.

blocks.text: A single stage is one mixer plus one settler. Feed (carrier plus solute) and solvent are stirred until the liquids touch everywhere, then left to settle into two layers: extract, rich in solvent, and raffinate, rich in carrier.

If the contact lasts long enough, the two leaving liquids are in equilibrium, so their compositions sit at opposite ends of one tie line on the triangular diagram. The total balance is F + S = E + R and the solute balance is F x_F + S y_S = E y_E + R x_R. Here F, S, E, R are mass flows in kg/h; x and y are solute mass fractions in carrier-rich and solvent-rich phases.

When carrier and solvent hardly dissolve in each other, carrier flow R stays constant. Use mass ratios: X = kg solute per kg carrier, Y = kg solute per kg solvent. Equilibrium is Y* = K X, with K in mass-ratio units.

blocks.where: X₀ and X₁ are kg solute per kg carrier in the feed and in the raffinate leaving stage 1; S is kg pure solvent fed to the stage; R is kg carrier in the feed; K is the equilibrium ratio Y*/X.

blocks.text: On the diagram, mark F and S, join them, and place mixture point M on FS so FM/MS = S/F by the lever rule. The tie line through M gives both phase compositions; its raffinate end read as a mass ratio is X₁.

sections.h3: Repeating the contact: the cross-current cascade

blocks.text: Cross-current means feed moves stage by stage while fresh solvent enters every stage. Each stage meets solvent with no solute, so the driving force is renewed.
X_n = X₀ / (1 + E)ⁿ   with   E = K·S/R
blocks.where: X_n is kg solute per kg carrier in the raffinate leaving stage n; X₀ is the feed ratio; E is the extraction factor (dimensionless); K is Y*/X; S is kg pure solvent per stage; R is kg carrier in the feed; n is the number of stages.

blocks.text: Stage n balance: R·X_{n−1} = R·X_n + S·Y_n with Y_n = K·X_n, so X_n = X_{n−1}/(1 + E). Applying n times gives the formula. E is solute leaving in extract divided by solute staying in raffinate for one stage.

items: Doubling n squares the surviving fraction; the fall is geometric, not linear.
A larger K or more solvent per stage raises E and lowers X_n.
Recovery is (X₀ − X_n)/X₀, not n times the single-stage recovery.

blocks.text: On the triangle each stage has its own M₁, M₂,… and tie line. Raffinate from one is feed to the next, joined to the fresh solvent point. With partially miscible liquids tie lines swing, so the formula fails and the diagram is stepped.

sections.h3: Splitting the solvent, efficiency, batch washing

blocks.text: With fixed total solvent, the split matters. For constant K, equal portions maximise the product of denominators (1 + E) and minimise X_n. Loading one stage and starving others leaves more solute.

The example uses 3 × 200 = 600 kg. All 600 kg in one stage gives X₁ = 0.3333/(1 + 2×600/375) = 0.0794 kg/kg, that is 29.8 kg left and 76.2% recovered, against 14.2 kg and 88.7% for the split. Three clean contacts beat one with the same total.

Real stages never reach equilibrium. Stage efficiency η is actual composition change divided by ideal-stage change. A common short-cut multiplies the equilibrium constant: K_eff = ηK. This is not the same as efficiency on composition change. With K replaced by η·K, n real stages give X_n = X₀/(1 + ηE)ⁿ, equivalent to n·ln(1 + ηE)/ln(1 + E) ideal stages — about 2.3 when η = 0.7 and E = 1.07. The simpler rule ideal stages = η × real stages is a separate overall stage efficiency.

Batch extraction is the same arithmetic in one vessel: charge feed and solvent, stir, settle, draw off extract, repeat with fresh solvent. Two washes of 100 kg beat one wash of 200 kg by the same reason.

figure.caption: Feed walks from stage 1 to stage 3 while clean solvent enters every stage, so each contact starts with zero solute in the solvent and the raffinate gets progressively leaner.

spec.title: Three-stage cross-current train
spec.aria: Feed passes from stage 1 to stage 3 while a separate stream of fresh solvent enters every stage, so each contact starts with clean solvent.

examples.question: 500 kg of a solution containing 125 kg solute and 375 kg carrier is extracted in three cross-current stages, each using 200 kg of pure solvent. The distribution coefficient is constant at K = 2.0 on a solute-free mass-ratio basis (Y = 2X). Find the solute left in the final raffinate and the percentage recovered.
steps: Carrier and solvent immiscible: R = 375 kg, S = 200 kg per stage.
Feed mass ratio: X₀ = 125/375 = 0.3333 kg solute per kg carrier.
Extraction factor per stage: E = K·S/R = 2.0 × 200/375 = 1.0667.
Final raffinate ratio: X₃ = 0.3333/8.8270 = 0.03776 kg solute per kg carrier.
examples.answer: The final raffinate holds 14.16 kg of solute, so 88.67% has been recovered in three cross-current stages.

traps: Putting all 600 kg in one stage gives 29.76 kg left and 76.2% recovery, not 14.16 kg. Check if the solvent is split.
Feeding S as total solvent and R as feed mass. Use R = feed − solute when phases are immiscible.
Using mass fractions x,y where K is on mass ratios X,Y. Convert: X = x/(1 − x).
Inverting K. Y = K X, not X = K Y.
Treating n stages as n times single-stage recovery; the fall is geometric, and η < 1 needs more real stages.

quiz.q: Define the extraction factor E for a cross-current stage and state its units.
quiz.a: E = K·S/R, where K = Y*/X is the mass-ratio distribution coefficient, S is kg pure solvent per stage and R is kg carrier in the feed. It is dimensionless and equals the solute in the extract divided by the solute left in the raffinate for one ideal stage.

quiz.q: Why does three times 200 kg of solvent remove more solute than one charge of 600 kg?
quiz.a: Each portion enters with zero solute, so Y* = K·X_n stays low and driving force is renewed; only later stages see lean raffinate. Three denominators 2.0667 multiply to 8.827, while one stage with 600 kg gives 4.2.

quiz.q: A feed has X₀ = 0.4 kg solute per kg carrier. K = 1.5 and S/R = 1.0. Find X after two cross-current stages.
400 kg of solution containing 20% solute by mass is washed twice with 150 kg of pure solvent each time. K = 3.0. Find the solute left and the percentage recovered.
A student puts 400 kg of solvent in stage 1 and 100 kg in each of stages 2 and 3, keeping the total at 600 kg. Is this better than three equal 200 kg portions?
quiz.a: No. The denominators are 3.1333, 1.5333 and 1.5333, whose product is 7.367 against 8.827 for equal portions. For constant K, equal splitting maximises the product of denominators and minimises X₃.

quiz.q: What is stage efficiency in extraction?
quiz.a: The actual change in phase composition divided by the change an ideal equilibrium stage would give. A common short-cut replaces K by η·K, but that is an approximation, not the same as composition-change efficiency.

quiz.q: On the triangular diagram, how is the mixture point M found for one stage, and what follows from it?
quiz.a: Join the feed point F and the solvent point S, and place M on that line so that FM/MS = S/F by the lever rule. The tie line through M gives the extract and raffinate compositions leaving that stage; the raffinate end becomes the feed for the next stage.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry rarely runs large cross-current trains because they need more solvent and give a dilute extract; counter-current contact dominates there. The idea survives in batch washing, in sample preparation where a solid is extracted repeatedly with fresh solvent, and in small hydrometallurgical lots. The same recursion, written with E as the absorption or stripping factor, appears in tray absorbers and in the Kremser equation. Search next for cross-current leaching, multiple-contact batch extraction, and the Kremser equation as the counter-current cousin.
